pumac-2023-team-01.title: Exactly one hump means unimodal
pumac-2023-team-01.body:
A hump is a local maximum (the ends count with one neighbor). A permutation has exactly one local maximum iff it increases up to the position of $n$ and then decreases (any descent followed later by an ascent creates a valley and hence another local maximum). Such a permutation is determined by deciding for each of $1,\dots,n-1$ whether it lies left or right of $n$: $2^{n-1}$ permutations. So $P_n=\dfrac{2^{n-1}}{n!}$.

$P_n$ is a unit fraction iff $n!/2^{n-1}$ is an integer, i.e. $v_2(n!)\ge n-1$. By Legendre, $v_2(n!)=n-s_2(n)$ where $s_2(n)$ is the binary digit sum, so we need $s_2(n)=1$: $n$ is a power of $2$. For $n\le2020$: $1,2,4,\dots,1024$, which is $11$ values.

**Answer: 11**

pumac-2023-team-02.title: Fibonacci recurrence for $1/\sqrt r$
pumac-2023-team-02.body:
Two circles of radii $r,s$ tangent to each other and to a line on the same side touch the line at points $2\sqrt{rs}$ apart. For $\Gamma_n$ squeezed between $\Gamma_{n-2},\Gamma_{n-1}$ and $\ell$:
$$2\sqrt{r_{n-2}r_{n-1}}=2\sqrt{r_{n-2}r_n}+2\sqrt{r_{n-1}r_n}\iff\frac1{\sqrt{r_n}}=\frac1{\sqrt{r_{n-1}}}+\frac1{\sqrt{r_{n-2}}}.$$
Let $a_n=1/\sqrt{r_n}$: $a_1=\sqrt2$, $a_2=2\sqrt2$, and $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$, so $a_n=\sqrt2\,F_{n+1}$ and $a_{10}=\sqrt2\,F_{11}=89\sqrt2$. Then $r_{10}=\frac1{2\cdot89^2}=\frac1{15842}$ and $a+b=15843$.

**Answer: 15843**

pumac-2023-team-03.title: Case analysis
pumac-2023-team-03.body:
Write $f=ax^2+bx+c$ with $1\le a\le10$, $0\le b,c\le10$.

*Case 1: $b=0$ or $c=0$.* Then $f$ itself has at most two nonzero coefficients (take $g=1$). Count: $10\cdot(11+11-1)=210$.

*Case 2: $b,c\ge1$.* We need $f\mid h$ with $h=x^i(ux^m+v)$, $i+m\le3$, over $\mathbb Q$ (then clear denominators to get $g\in\mathbb Z[x]$). Since $f(0)\ne0$, $f$ is coprime to $x$ and must divide $ux^m+v$ with $m\le3$ ($u\neq0$). Reduce $x^m$ modulo $f$: $x^2\equiv-\frac bax-\frac ca$ has a nonzero $x$-coefficient, so $m=1,2$ fail; $x^3\equiv\frac{b^2-ac}{a^2}x+\frac{bc}{a^2}$ has zero $x$-coefficient iff $b^2=ac$. So the condition is $b^2=ac$. The triples $(a,b,c)\in[1,10]^3$ with $b^2=ac$: $b=1:1$; $b=2:3$; $b=3:3$; $b=4:3$; $b=5:1$; $b=6:3$; $b=7:1$; $b=8:1$; $b=9:1$; $b=10:1$, total $18$.

Total $210+18=228$.

**Answer: 228**

pumac-2023-team-04.title: Lucas' theorem
pumac-2023-team-04.body:
By Lucas' theorem mod $2$, $\binom nx$ is odd iff every binary digit $1$ of $x$ is also a $1$ of $n$. So $x$ may use only the positions where both $1515$ and $1975$ have a $1$:
$$1515=10111101011_2,\quad1975=11110110111_2,\quad\text{common }1\text{s: }2^{10},2^8,2^7,2^5,2^1,2^0.$$
We want the largest such $x<1000$; we cannot use $2^{10}=1024$, so $x=2^8+2^7+2^5+2+1=256+128+32+3=419$.

**Answer: 419**

pumac-2023-team-05.title: Euler product
pumac-2023-team-05.body:
$\varphi(q)/q^2$ is multiplicative and every $q\in S$ factors uniquely over the five primes, so the sum is $\prod_{p\in\{2,3,5,7,11\}}\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\varphi(p^k)}{p^{2k}}$. For each $p$:
$$1+\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{p^{k-1}(p-1)}{p^{2k}}=1+\frac{p-1}{p}\sum_{k\ge1}p^{-k}=1+\frac{p-1}{p}\cdot\frac1{p-1}=\frac{p+1}p.$$
The product is $\frac32\cdot\frac43\cdot\frac65\cdot\frac87\cdot\frac{12}{11}=\frac{1152}{385}$, and $a+b=1537$.

**Answer: 1537**

pumac-2023-team-06.title: Which primes work
pumac-2023-team-06.body:
Reduce the sum mod $p$: $\sum x_i\equiv1+2+\dots+p\equiv\frac{p(p+1)}2\equiv0\pmod p$ for odd $p$, so $p\mid2022=2\cdot3\cdot337$ and $p=3$ or $337$. For $p=337$ the minimum possible sum is $\sum_{i<p}i=\frac{p(p-1)}2=56616>2022$, so $f=0$. For $p=2$: $x_1$ is odd and $x_2$ even, so the sum is odd, $f(2)=0$.

For $p=3$: $x_1=1+3y_1$, $x_2=2+3y_2$, $x_3=3y_3$ with $y_i\ge0$, so $3+3(y_1+y_2+y_3)=2022$, i.e. $y_1+y_2+y_3=673$: $\binom{675}2=227\,475$ solutions. The remainder mod $1000$ is $475$.

**Answer: 475**

pumac-2023-team-07.title: Vieta and independence
pumac-2023-team-07.body:
The sum of squares of coefficients is $1+p^2+q^2+r^2$ with $p=-(a+b+c)$, $q=ab+bc+ca$, $r=-abc$. Let $\mu=E[a]= rac72$ and $
u=E[a^2]= rac{91}6$. By independence:
- $E[p^2]=E[\sum a^2+2\sum ab]=3
u+6\mu^2$,
- $E[q^2]=E[\sum a^2b^2+2abc(a+b+c)]=3
u^2+6
u\mu^2$,
- $E[r^2]=
u^3$.

Total: $1+3
u+6\mu^2+3
u^2+6
u\mu^2+
u^3= rac{1169335}{216}$ (the numerator and $216$ are coprime). So $m+n=1169551\equiv551\pmod{1000}$.

**Answer: 551**

pumac-2023-team-08.title: Subtract three corner triangles
pumac-2023-team-08.body:
The hexagon $DNFEML$ is $\triangle ABC$ minus the triangles $BND$, $CLM$, $AEF$. Let $[ABC]=\Delta$; Heron: $s=9$, $\Delta=\sqrt{9\cdot4\cdot2\cdot3}=6\sqrt6$. By the law of cosines $\cos A=\frac{36+25-49}{60}=\frac15$ and $\cos B=\frac{25+49-36}{70}=\frac{19}{35}$.
- $\triangle CLM\sim\triangle CBA$ with ratio $\frac12$: $[CLM]=\frac14\Delta$.
- $\triangle AEF\sim\triangle ABC$ with ratio $\cos A$: $[AEF]=\cos^2A\,\Delta=\frac1{25}\Delta$.
- $N$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse $AB$ of the right triangle $ABD$, so $[BND]=\frac12[ABD]=\frac12\cdot\frac{BD}{BC}\Delta=\frac12\cdot\frac{AB\cos B}{BC}\Delta=\frac12\cdot\frac{19/7}{7}\Delta=\frac{19}{98}\Delta$.

Hence the area is $\Delta\left(1-\frac{19}{98}-\frac14-\frac1{25}\right)=6\sqrt6\cdot\frac{2529}{4900}=\frac{7587\sqrt6}{2450}$, and $x+y+z=7587+6+2450=10043$.

**Answer: 10043**

pumac-2023-team-09.title: Symmetric functions and AM-GM
pumac-2023-team-09.body:
Let the roots be $x_1,\dots,x_4$ and $e_k$ the elementary symmetric polynomials. By Vieta $U=-Pe_1$, $M=Pe_2$, $A=-Pe_3$, $C=Pe_4$. Expanding,
$$e_2^2=m_{22}+2m_{211}+6e_4,\qquad e_1e_3=m_{211}+4e_4,$$
where $m_{22}=\sum_{i<j}x_i^2x_j^2$ and $m_{211}=\sum x_i^2x_jx_k$. Therefore
$$M^2-2UA+zPC=P^2\bigl(e_2^2-2e_1e_3+ze_4\bigr)=P^2\bigl(m_{22}+(z-2)e_4\bigr).$$
By AM-GM on the six terms of $m_{22}$ (each $x_i$ occurs in three of the terms with exponent $2$, so their product is $e_4^6$ and their geometric mean is $e_4$), $m_{22}\ge6e_4$, with strict inequality for distinct roots. So for $z\ge-4$ the expression is $>P^2(z+4)e_4\ge0$. If $z<-4$, taking four roots very close together makes $m_{22}/e_4\to6$ and the expression negative. So the smallest $z$ is $-4$, and $z^2=16$.

**Answer: 16**

pumac-2023-team-10.title: Closed form of $\sum k\cos k\theta$
pumac-2023-team-10.body:
For $\theta\not\equiv0\pmod{2\pi}$ (differentiating the geometric series, or summation by parts),
$$\sum_{k=1}^Nk\cos k\theta=\frac{(N+1)\cos N\theta-N\cos(N+1)\theta-1}{2(1-\cos\theta)}.$$
(Check: $N=1$ gives $\cos\theta$.) Here $\theta=\frac{4\pi}{4041}$, $N=2020$: $N\theta=\frac{8080\pi}{4041}=2\pi-\frac{2\pi}{4041}$ and $(N+1)\theta=2\pi+\frac{2\pi}{4041}$, so both cosines equal $\cos\frac{2\pi}{4041}$ and the numerator is $2021C-2020C-1=C-1$. The denominator is $4\sin^2\frac{2\pi}{4041}$. So the sum is $\dfrac{\cos\frac{2\pi}{4041}-1}{4\sin^2\frac{2\pi}{4041}}$: $a=1,b=1,c=4,p=2,q=4041$, and $a+b+c+p+q=4049$.

**Answer: 4049**

pumac-2023-team-11.title: Cross ratio
pumac-2023-team-11.body:
A Möbius transformation preserves cross ratios. With $w=f(4)$ and the points $1,2,3\mapsto i,-1,-i$:
$$\frac{4-2}{4-3}\cdot\frac{1-3}{1-2}=\frac{w+1}{w+i}\cdot\frac{i-(-i)}{i-(-1)},\quad\text{i.e.}\quad4=\frac{w+1}{w+i}\cdot\frac{2i}{1+i}.$$
So $\frac{w+1}{w+i}=\frac{2(1+i)}{i}=2-2i$, giving $w+1=(2-2i)(w+i)$, $w(-1+2i)=1+2i$, and
$$w=\frac{1+2i}{-1+2i}=\frac{(1+2i)(-1-2i)}{5}=\frac{3-4i}5.$$
Real part $\frac35$: $m^2+n^2=9+25=34$.

**Answer: 34**

pumac-2023-team-12.title: Shallow diagonals of Pascal's triangle
pumac-2023-team-12.body:
Let $T$ be the sum of $\binom ij$ over all $i,j\ge0$ with $i+j\le20$ (with $\binom ij=0$ for $j>i$). Grouping by $s=i+j$, the sum along a shallow diagonal is $\sum_j\binom{s-j}j=F_{s+1}$ (Fibonacci), so
$$T=\sum_{s=0}^{20}F_{s+1}=F_{23}-1=28657-1=28656.$$
The pairs with $i\le9$ are all included in $T$ with every $0\le j\le i$ (since $i+j\le18\le20$), contributing $\sum_{i=0}^92^i=1023$. Our sum is the rest: $28656-1023=27633$.

**Answer: 27633**

pumac-2023-team-13.title: Similar triangles and lengths
pumac-2023-team-13.body:
Rename $T,D$ as $A,C$ (so $a=BC=8$, $b=CA=7$, $c=AB=6$); $M$ is the midpoint of arc $BC$, $Y=AB\cap MC$, $X=AC\cap MB$.

*Similarity.* $\angle YZB=\angle YMB=\angle XMC=\angle XZC$ (circles $YBMZ$, $XCMZ$ and vertical angles at $M$), and $\angle BYZ=\angle BMZ=\angle XCZ$. So $\triangle ZYB\sim\triangle ZCX$ and $\dfrac xy=\left(\dfrac{YB}{XC}\right)^2$.

*Lengths.* $\triangle YBM\sim\triangle YCA$ gives $\frac{YB}{YC}=\frac{YM}{YA}=\frac{MB}{b}$. With $YC=YM+MC$, $YA=YB+c$, $MC=MB$ and $k=MB/b$: $YB=k^2(b+c)/(1-k^2)=\dfrac{MB^2(b+c)}{b^2-MB^2}$. Symmetrically $XC=\dfrac{MB^2(b+c)}{c^2-MB^2}$. So $\frac{YB}{XC}=\frac{c^2-MB^2}{b^2-MB^2}$.

*$MB$.* $MB=\frac{a}{2\cos(A/2)}$, so $MB^2=\frac{a^2}{2(1+\cos A)}=\frac{a^2bc}{(b+c)^2-a^2}$. Substituting,
$$\frac{YB}{XC}=\frac{c\,(c(b+c)-a^2)}{b\,(b(b+c)-a^2)}=\frac{6\cdot14}{7\cdot27}=\frac49.$$
Thus $\frac xy=\frac{16}{81}$ and $p+q=97$. (A coordinate computation confirms $[YBZ]/[XDZ]=16/81$.)

**Answer: 97**

pumac-2023-team-14.title: Separate horizontal and vertical moves
pumac-2023-team-14.body:
Let $n=7$ (so $2n=14$ jumps). Suppose $2k$ of the jumps are horizontal and $2(n-k)$ vertical. The horizontal moves alone form a walk on $x\ge0$ returning to $0$ in $2k$ steps: $C_k$ ways (Catalan), the vertical ones $C_{n-k}$ ways, and the positions of the horizontal jumps among the $2n$ can be chosen in $\binom{2n}{2k}$ ways. So the number of walks is
$$\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{2n}{2k}C_kC_{n-k}.$$
Each term equals $\dfrac{(2n)!}{k!(k+1)!(n-k)!(n-k+1)!}=C_n\cdot\dfrac1{n+1}\binom{n+1}k\binom{n+1}{k+1}$. By Vandermonde $\sum_k\binom{n+1}k\binom{n+1}{n-k}=\binom{2n+2}n$, so the sum is $C_n\cdot\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n+2}{n}=C_nC_{n+1}$. For $n=7$: $C_7C_8=429\cdot1430=613470$. (A direct dynamic-programming count agrees.)

**Answer: 613470**

pumac-2023-team-15.title: Recurrences and the 3-adic valuation
pumac-2023-team-15.body:
Call such strings *bifix-free*. A string with a border (a prefix equal to a suffix) has a border of length $\le n/2$ (a shortest border has length $\le n/2$, otherwise the two copies overlap and yield a shorter border). Consequently:

- Inserting any digit in the exact middle of a bifix-free string of length $2n$ gives a bifix-free string of length $2n+1$, and deleting the middle digit reverses it, so $a_{2n+1}=3a_{2n}$.
- For length $2n-1\to2n$: insert a digit in position $n$ ($3$ ways). The new string has no border of length $<n$; it either is bifix-free or its two halves coincide and are themselves bifix-free of length $n$. This gives $3a_{2n-1}=a_{2n}+a_n$, i.e. $a_{2n}=3a_{2n-1}-a_n$.

With $a_1=3,a_2=6$ (checked by brute force for $n\le8$: $3,6,18,48,144,414,1242,3678$). Claim: $v_3(a_n)=s_2(n)$, the number of binary $1$'s of $n$. This holds for $n=1,2$; assume it for all smaller indices. If $n+1$ is odd, $a_{n+1}=3a_n$ and $s_2(n+1)=s_2(n)+1$. If $n+1=2m$, then $a_{2m}=3a_{2m-1}-a_m$ with $v_3(3a_{2m-1})=1+s_2(2m-1)=2+s_2(m-1)\ge1+s_2(m)>s_2(m)=v_3(a_m)$, so $v_3(a_{2m})=v_3(a_m)=s_2(m)=s_2(2m)$.

$2023=11111100111_2$ has $9$ ones, so $m=9$ (also confirmed by computing $a_{2023}$ exactly from the recurrences).

**Answer: 9**
